set.st: Several versions of one legend. Soldiers from Fort Crawford crossing to McGregor's landing with $8,000 in gold to pay the Fort Atkinson garrison were killed by Indians after burying it on a hill, said to be the Heights; other tellings have a canoe of gold sunk in the Mississippi, a sack buried near Fort Crawford, or $80,000 buried by four of Col. Zachary Taylor's soldiers near North McGregor. A Decorah paper's 1905 version put the sum at $890,000 in four bags of soldiers' pay from Colonel Taylor's stockade in 1830, hidden from the Indians by four men and 'never found about the bluff'. Early settlers hunted the hills, and in 1913 a man with a 'gold magnet' came to McGregor to search. In 1937 a girl found an 1851 $10 gold piece on a Mississippi river hill south of McGregor; years earlier three children had found a $20 gold piece on the same side hill a little to the north, and the paper suggested both had washed down from a cache higher in the bluff. A farm west of McGregor was nicknamed the 'Gold Mine' farm for all the digging there. Pin is approximate, not the spot itself. The 1905 wire as printed: in 1830 four bags of gold coin, $80,000 for the soldiers' pay, reached Col. Zachary Taylor's fort ('Fort McKay'). Fearing attack, he sent four trusted men to hide them; the fort was attacked, and after days of fighting the four were found dead. A scrap of paper near the body of the man called Mercierre said the money was 'buried on the highest of the bluffs across from the place where they were found'. Parties searched and found nothing; 'hundreds of people have worked by the day' on the lonely bluff near North McGregor, and in 1905 a premium was being offered. The 1906 syndicate feature printed the note as 'ON HIGHEST BLUFF ACROSS FROM FORT IN 4 PILES EACH 20,000 PIERRE MERCIERRE' and put Fort McKay 'near where the little town of North McGregor, Iowa, now stands'. In Feb 1905 hundreds were digging on the bluff, and Taylor's parties dug for days in 1906; 'never a trace was found'.
